name: TLV9062IDR
title: TLV9061, TLV9062, TLV9064: 10 MHz rail-to-rail CMOS op amps, with shutdown versions
summary: Single, dual and quad CMOS operational amplifiers for 1.8 V to 5.5 V supplies. Inputs reach 100 mV past both rails and the outputs swing to the rails. They give 10 MHz gain bandwidth and 6.5 V/µs on 538 µA per channel, with 0.5 pA bias current and ±0.3 mV typical offset; they are unity-gain stable, filter RF at the inputs and do not phase-reverse. The S versions add active-low shutdown pins that cut the supply current below 1 µA and leave the outputs high impedance.

circuits.title: Single-pole low-pass filter with gain
circuits.description: An RC network, R1 in series and C1 to ground, filters the input before the noninverting input; RG from the inverting input to ground and RF from the output back to the inverting input give a noninverting gain of 1 + RF / RG. The -3 dB corner is 1 / (2π R1 C1).

circuits.title: Low-side current sense
circuits.description: Load current from VBUS passes through ZLOAD and returns to ground through a 0.1 Ω shunt. The shunt voltage, at most 100 mV at 1 A, drives the noninverting input; RF = 165 kΩ from the output to the inverting input and RG = 3.4 kΩ from there to ground set a gain of about 49.5 V/V, so the output runs from about 0 V to 4.95 V over 0 A to 1 A. The amplifier runs from a single 5 V supply.
notes: Design targets: 0 A to 1 A load current, 4.95 V output at full scale, 100 mV largest shunt voltage.

circuits.title: Series input resistor limiting overload current
circuits.description: A unity-gain follower, output tied to the inverting input, whose noninverting input is fed through 5 kΩ. If the input is driven past a supply rail, the resistor holds the current into the input clamp diodes to the 10 mA limit. The resistor adds thermal noise at the input.

circuits.title: Two noninverting amplifiers (layout example)
circuits.description: Both channels of a TLV9062 in the 8-pin package as noninverting amplifiers: each input goes to IN+, RG runs from IN- to ground and RF from IN- to the output. A low-ESR ceramic bypass capacitor goes from each supply pin to ground, as close to the package as possible; RF and RG sit next to the inverting input.
notes: Bypass capacitors are 0.1 µF low-ESR ceramic.
A ground plane lies on another layer.

operation.text: TLV9061 has one amplifier, TLV9062 two and TLV9064 four; TLV9061S, TLV9062S and TLV9064S add shutdown inputs. All are unity-gain stable CMOS op amps for 1.8 V to 5.5 V with inputs and outputs that reach the rails, a built-in RFI/EMI filter at the inputs, and no phase reversal when the inputs are overdriven. Every channel count comes in tiny X2SON or X2QFN packages as well as SOIC, MSOP, SOT-23 and TSSOP.
The amplifier drives 100 pF directly; because its open-loop output impedance is resistive, heavier capacitive loads are easier to stabilize.
In shutdown the S versions draw typically under 1 µA.

The amplifiers are low-power op amps for general use from 1.8 V to 5.5 V. The input common-mode range takes in both rails, so they suit almost any single-supply circuit, and the rail-to-rail swing widens dynamic range on low supplies. The bandwidth is enough to drive the sample-and-hold input of an ADC.

The common-mode range runs 100 mV past both rails over the whole 1.8 V to 5.5 V supply range. Two input pairs share it: a P-channel pair covers from 200 mV below V- to about (V+) - 1.4 V, and an N-channel pair from about (V+) - 1.4 V to 200 mV above V+. Both pairs conduct in a band typically (V+) - 1.2 V to (V+) - 1 V, 200 mV wide; with process spread that band can lie anywhere from (V+) - 1.4 V to (V+) - 1.2 V at the low end up to (V+) - 1 V to (V+) - 0.8 V at the high end. Inside it offset, offset drift, PSRR, CMRR and THD can be worse than elsewhere.

The output stage is class AB, built from common-source transistors, and swings rail to rail: into 10 kΩ the output comes within 15 mV of either rail at any supply voltage. Other loads change how close it gets.

Internal filtering reduces the effect of RF interference from radios and from crowded mixed-signal boards. EMIRR at the noninverting input was measured from 10 MHz to 6 GHz; values at common frequencies are in the EMIRR table.

When the input or the gain drives the output past its range, the output transistors saturate and need time for their charge carriers to return before the amplifier works linearly again; it then slews at its normal rate. The delay out of an overload is the recovery time plus the slewing time. Recovery takes about 200 ns.

On the S versions the active-low SHDN inputs put the amplifier in a low-power standby drawing typically under 1 µA. The inputs are referred to V-; the threshold is about 800 mV typical above V- and does not move with supply voltage, and it has hysteresis. A valid low is V- to V- + 0.2 V and a valid high is V- + 1.2 V to V+. The pins are CMOS inputs of high impedance with no internal pull-up, so each must be driven or tied high or low, never left floating. Each channel of the dual has its own pin; the quad's channels switch in pairs. Enable from full shutdown takes 10 µs and disable 6 µs. A disabled output is high impedance, so the part can act as a gated amplifier or share an analog output bus. Turn-off time grows with load resistance; the specified time needs the 10 kΩ load to mid-supply (VS / 2), and with no load it is much longer.
The amplifiers operate with a supply between 1.8 V (±0.9 V) and 5.5 V (±2.75 V). The S versions are shut down while a valid logic low is on the shutdown pin.
10 MHz bandwidth and 6.5 V/µs slew rate on 538 µA per channel; for DC work, 10 nV/√Hz noise at 10 kHz, low bias current and 0.3 mV typical offset.

The gain depends only on the ratio of RF to RG. Their absolute values set the impedance level, which decides current drain, how much stray capacitance matters and some other behaviour; no single level suits every system.
Operation is specified from 1.8 V to 5.5 V (±0.9 V to ±2.75 V), with many limits holding from -40°C to 125°C. More than 6 V across the supply can damage the part permanently.

Put 0.1 µF capacitors near the supply pins so that noise on a noisy or high-impedance supply stays out. Low-ESR ceramic parts go from each supply pin to ground, as near the package as possible; a single-supply design needs only the one on V+.

Every pin has internal ESD protection; at the inputs and output it is mainly steering diodes to the supply pins. These diodes also protect against input overdrive as long as the current stays within 10 mA. A series resistor in the driven input limits that current; it adds thermal noise at the input, so keep it small where noise matters.

Separate analog and digital grounds and watch the ground current path; a ground plane on one or more layers spreads heat and reduces EMI pickup. Run input traces as far from supply and output traces as possible, and if they must cross a noisy trace, cross it at 90 degrees rather than in parallel. Place external parts close to the package; RF and RG next to the inverting input keep its parasitic capacitance low. Keep input traces short. Guarding critical traces with a ring driven at low impedance cuts leakage from nearby traces at other voltages.
Clean the board after assembly. Moisture absorbed into the plastic package can shift performance, so after an aqueous wash bake the assembly; 30 minutes at 85°C is enough in most cases.
On the DSG (WSON) and RTE (WQFN) packages the exposed thermal pad connects to V-, and it is soldered to the board for heat and mechanical strength.
